  – Episodic frontal headaches during computer or meeting work; nausea present; no radiation.  
  – Reduced appetite with ~5 lb unintentional weight loss.  
  – Intermittent tingling (“quick pricking”) in both hands; no leg involvement.  
  – Daily episodes of palpitations, sometimes when entering elevator.  
  – Occasional feeling of being “hot”/short of breath while seated at desk; no exercise limitation.  
  – Decreased libido, onset concurrent with job change.  
• Past medical history: “hyperthyroidism” (patient term) – takes thyroxine.  
• Medications: Thyroxine – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Allergies: Not stated.  
• Social: Lawyer in London; alcohol once weekly (2 glasses wine); non-smoker; denies recreational drug use.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Headaches  
   - Assessment: New-onset work-related tension-type headache vs stress-related vs thyroid dysfunction.  
   - Investigations: Neurologic examination at visit; consider visual acuity, fundoscopic exam.  
   - Treatment: Pending in-person review; analgesic advice deferred.

2. Reduced appetite & unintentional weight loss  
   - Assessment: Likely multifactorial (stress vs thyroid imbalance).  
   - Investigations: Weight/BMI measurement; thyroid function tests; basic metabolic panel.  
   - Treatment: Address underlying cause after results.

3. Bilateral hand tingling  
   - Assessment: Possible stress-related hyperventilation paresthesia vs peripheral neuropathy.  
   - Investigations: Neurologic exam; consider B12 if persists.

4. Palpitations  
   - Assessment: Possible anxiety/stress-induced tachycardia vs thyrotoxicosis.  
   - Investigations: Heart rate, blood pressure, ECG at clinic; thyroid function tests.  
   - Treatment: Dependent on findings.

5. Shortness of breath/feeling hot  
   - Assessment: Likely anxiety or thyrotoxicosis; rule out cardiopulmonary pathology.  
   - Investigations: Auscultation, oxygen saturation, thyroid panel.  
   - Treatment: To be guided by exam.

6. Loss of libido  
   - Assessment: Likely stress-related; endocrine contribution to be excluded.  
   - Investigations: Review thyroid results; additional hormonal work-up if indicated.

7. Thyroid disease follow-up  
   - Assessment: Possible inadequate or excessive thyroxine replacement (conflict with stated “hyperthyroidism”).  
   - Investigations: Thyroid function tests.  
   - Treatment: Adjust thyroxine dose as per results.  
   - Relevant referral: Endocrinology if results abnormal or symptoms persist.
